title: Where Does the Rain Go?
topic: Science and community: how a school can manage rainwater

listening.title: Mr. Ortiz explains the new rain garden
listening.context: You are in science class. Your teacher is explaining a project outside the school.
listening.purpose: Listen to find out what the rain garden does and what happens in order.
script: Good morning, scientists. Last month, our school parking lot flooded after a big storm. Today I want to explain why that happened, and what we are building to help.

Pavement cannot absorb water. So when rain lands on the parking lot, it becomes runoff. The runoff rushes downhill and collects at the lowest corner, near the front doors. That is where the flood started.

A rain garden gives runoff somewhere to go. First, a small channel guides the water off the pavement. Second, the water slows down in a shallow bowl filled with plants. Third, the soil filters the water as it soaks in. Finally, the clean water reaches the ground below the school instead of flooding the doors.
Notice that we are not stopping the rain. We are changing where the water goes. Next week, you will measure how fast the garden absorbs water. Bring your science notebooks.

tasks.prompt: Put the rain garden steps in the order Mr. Ortiz described.

items.text: The soil filters the water as it soaks in.
A small channel guides water off the pavement.
The water slows down in a shallow bowl of plants.
Clean water reaches the ground below the school.

feedback.right: You tracked four steps in sequence. The speaker used First, Second, Third, and Finally to signal the order.
feedback.wrong: Listen for the signal words First, Second, Third, and Finally. They tell you the order. The steps are in the third part of the talk.

tasks.prompt: What is the main reason the parking lot flooded?

options.text: The storm was the biggest one in the school's history.
The soil near the front doors was too dry to hold water after the storm.
Pavement could not absorb the rain, so runoff collected near the doors.
The school did not have enough plants around the building to hold water.

feedback.right: Cause and effect: pavement cannot absorb water, so it becomes runoff and flows to the lowest corner.
feedback.wrong: Listen to the second part again. The speaker gives the cause with the words Pavement cannot absorb water. So...

distractors.a: adds a claim the speaker never made (biggest storm)
distractors.b: reverses the idea: the problem was pavement, not dry soil
distractors.d: mentions plants, but plants are part of the solution, not the cause

tasks.prompt: What does Mr. Ortiz mean when he says, “We are not stopping the rain. We are changing where the water goes”?

options.text: The garden will make storms smaller by growing more plants.
The school wants less rain to fall on the building each year.
The class will measure how much rain falls each day next week.
The garden gives water a safe path so it does not flood the doors.

feedback.right: You inferred the purpose of the project: the rain still falls, but the garden directs it.
feedback.wrong: Think about what the garden does with runoff. Which choice matches that job, not stopping the weather?

distractors.a: gives plants power over weather, which the talk never says
distractors.b: contradicts the sentence: the rain is not being reduced
distractors.c: is the next-week activity, not the meaning of the sentence

reading.title: Where Does the Rain Go?

visual.alt: A side view of two ground surfaces during rain. On the left, a parking lot: rain hits pavement, runs along the surface in a long arrow, and collects in a puddle at the doors. On the right, a rain garden: a channel carries water to a shallow bowl with plants, then arrows show water moving down through soil.
visual.caption: Figure 1. Rain on pavement (left) and rain in a rain garden (right).

passage: When rain falls on natural ground, most of it soaks in. The soil absorbs the water and plant roots hold it in place. Water that soaks in can also be filtered, which means the soil cleans it as it moves downward.

Cities and schools have a different problem. Pavement covers much of the ground, and pavement cannot absorb water. Rain runs across it as runoff, picking up oil, trash, and dirt along the way. When a lot of runoff reaches one place at the same time, a flood can begin.

Table 1 shows how much water three surfaces absorbed during a ten-minute test with the same amount of rain. Pavement absorbed almost nothing. The rain garden absorbed the most because its soil and plants gave the water time to soak in.
A rain garden does not stop the rain. It slows the water and gives it a place to go. Because the water soaks in near where it fell, there is less runoff, and fewer places flood.

pair.title: Paired text: A student's view
pair.text: I think our school should build a rain garden. Last month I walked through water up to my ankles to get inside. A garden would cost money and take space, but it would protect our doors and give students a place to study plants. The table shows that a rain garden absorbs far more water than a lawn, so it is worth the space.

tasks.prompt: In paragraph 2, what does the word runoff mean?

options.text: Water that soaks deep into the soil below the ground
Water that flows over the ground instead of soaking in
Rain that falls very fast during a big storm
A kind of hard ground used for parking lots

feedback.right: The sentence before the word gives the clue: rain “runs across” pavement, and pavement cannot absorb it.
feedback.wrong: Reread paragraph 2. Find the phrase that tells how rain moves across pavement. That is the meaning of runoff.

distractors.a: is the opposite: runoff does not soak in
distractors.c: describes speed, not where the water goes
distractors.d: confuses runoff with pavement, the surface it runs across

tasks.prompt: Which sentence from the text best shows why pavement causes floods? Pin the sentence, then answer.

feedback.right: That sentence names the cause (pavement cannot absorb water) and the effect (runoff collects and floods).
feedback.wrong: Look for the sentence that gives both a cause and what it leads to. Try paragraph 2.

tasks.prompt: Using Table 1, how much more water did the rain garden absorb than the lawn?

options.text: 30 liters more
55 liters more
85 liters more
30 liters less

feedback.right: 85 minus 55 equals 30. You used the table as evidence and compared two rows.
feedback.wrong: Find the Absorbed number for Rain garden (85) and for Lawn (55). Subtract to compare.

distractors.b: is the lawn's own number, not a comparison
distractors.c: is the rain garden's own number, not a comparison

tasks.prompt: How does the student's opinion use information from the informational text?

options.text: The student repeats the full definition of runoff that appears in the text.
The student disagrees with the text and says pavement does not cause floods.
The student points to the table: a rain garden absorbs more than a lawn.
The student says a rain garden will stop the rain from falling on the school.

feedback.right: The opinion connects a personal experience to data from the first text. That is how an argument uses evidence.
feedback.wrong: Find the last sentence of the student's opinion. Which data does it point to?

distractors.b: the student agrees with the text about floods
distractors.d: repeats the misconception the text corrects: gardens change where water goes

speaking.title: Explain the picture to a classmate
speaking.prompt: Look at Figure 1. Explain to a classmate why the parking lot floods and how a rain garden helps. Use the picture to give details.
planning: What happens to rain on pavement?
What does the rain garden do first, next, and last?
frames: Rain falls on the ___, and it cannot ___.
A rain garden helps because first ___, then ___, so ___.
speaking.model: In the picture, rain lands on the pavement. Pavement cannot absorb water, so the water becomes runoff and collects near the doors, which causes a flood. A rain garden helps because first a channel carries the water to a bowl, then the plants slow it down, and finally the soil filters it. As a result, the water soaks in and the doors stay dry.

checks.text: I explained what causes the flood and what the garden does.
I used details from the picture and words like runoff, absorb, or filter.
I connected ideas with words like because, so, first, or finally.

speaking.selfCheckNote: Self-check only. The lab cannot hear or score your words. Ask your teacher or a partner to rate your recording with the Speaking rubric.

writing.title: Should our school build a rain garden?
writing.prompt: Write a short argument for or against building a rain garden at your school. State your claim, give reasons, and use evidence from the reading, including Table 1.
frames: I believe our school should ___ because ___.
writing.modelDraft: I believe our school should build a rain garden because it protects the front doors. According to Table 1, a rain garden absorbed 85 liters, but a lawn absorbed only 55 liters. Pavement absorbs almost nothing, so runoff makes floods. Some people say a garden takes too much space. However, the garden keeps students safe and dry, so the space is worth it.
writing.firstDraftExample: Rain garden is good. It is have plants. Water go in the ground. I like it.
